title: I Survived 100 Days as a Monkey Science Didn't Know Existed
description: Animal Secrets #27 — What if you were a young red howler monkey in the southern Amazon, leaving home to find a new family across a forest cut into islands? A Day 1 to Day 100 survival story (fiction), but every number is real. On 30 Oct 2026 scientists named the Mato Grosso red howler, the first new howler species in 84 years — and it may already be on the brink.

scenes.say: My hands are on the ground. For a monkey like me, that's terrible news.
I'm in the middle of a red dirt road. And something huge is roaring toward me.
I'm a young red howler monkey from the southern Amazon, in Brazil. This is a what if story, but every number in it is real.
How did I end up down here? And what did scientists say about me by the end, on Day 100? Let me take you back. Day 1.

scenes.label: Southern Amazon, Brazil
scenes.say: Day 1. Dawn, deep in the forest. Mist on the trees. And my family is about to wake up the whole world.
Okay, so here's our morning routine. We don't sing. We roar. All of us, together, from the treetops.

scenes.label: Built-in speaker
scenes.say: My dad has a giant hollow bone in his throat, the hyoid. It works like a built-in speaker.

scenes.label: Heard 4.8 km away
scenes.say: Under the right conditions, a howler's call can be heard about three miles away. That's 4.8 kilometers of forest.
Why roar? Because the neighbors roar back. It's how groups say 'this patch is ours' without ever having to fight.
There are eight of us. Dad, my mom, two aunts, my cousins, and me. Our whole world is one small patch of forest.
Day 4. You want to know our big secret? We're incredibly lazy. And it keeps us alive.
We eat leaves. Mostly leaves. And leaves are terrible fuel. Tough, stringy, and low in energy.
Bacteria in our gut ferment them slowly, so we save energy the only way we can. We rest.

scenes.label: 15+ hours resting
scenes.say: Red howlers can spend over 15 hours a day just resting, sitting, lying on branches. I'm not lazy. I'm efficient.
And we're picky. Some mature leaves carry toxins, so we never eat too much of one kind in one sitting.
Young leaves are the best. Softer and easier to digest. My mom always finds them first.

scenes.label: 400 m a day
scenes.say: Because leaves are everywhere, we barely travel. A howler group might move only about 400 meters a day. That's it.
A home range can be around 31 hectares for a whole group. Tiny. Which is great, until someone cuts your forest in half.
Day 9. I'm sunbathing on a high branch. Then my aunt barks a warning, and every monkey goes silent.
A shadow slides across the leaves. Huge. It's a harpy eagle, and monkeys like us are on its menu.

scenes.label: Up to 6.5 kg prey
scenes.say: Here's the scary part. Scientists once watched a harpy take an adult howler weighing up to six and a half kilos.
Mom yanks me into a thick tangle of vines. We freeze. No roar, no movement, not even a breath.
The eagle circles once, twice, and glides away. My heart is pounding. Lesson one: open branches get you killed.
Day 15. The rain is gone. Totally gone. Trees start dropping their leaves, and the forest turns yellow and pink.
Pretty, sure. But fewer leaves means less food for leaf eaters like us, and fewer places to hide.

scenes.label: 95% less rain
scenes.say: And this is a bad year. An El Niño drought. Near Manaus, rain in August 2026 was 95 percent below normal.
Our group moves less and rests more. Then, one evening, I realize something. I'm getting too big for this family.
Day 21. Here's a strange fact about howlers. Unlike most monkeys in the Americas, both young males and young females usually leave home.
Nobody chases me out. It's just time. To have a family of my own, I have to find a new group.
So at sunrise I give my family one last roar, and I climb away into trees I've never seen before.
Alone. No warning barks. No mom to grab me. Can a young howler survive by herself out here? We're about to find out.
Day 26. First problem: where do I sleep without getting eaten? I pick a giant kapok tree.

scenes.label: 15–20 m up
scenes.say: Howlers usually sleep high, around 15 to 20 meters up, clustered together. I don't have a cluster anymore. Just me.
And we avoid bare, leafless trees at night. No leaves means no cover. A kinkajou squeaks past me in the dark.
Below me, something heavy walks through the dry leaves. Slow. Silent. I don't look down. I already know it's a jaguar.
Jaguars are on the list of howler predators, and staying high is how we avoid them. So I stay up, very still, until the sky turns gray.
Day 31. I hit a wall. Not a wall of stone, a wall of water. A river.
Here's the twist. Big Amazon rivers are so hard to cross that they've split howlers into separate species over millions of years.
Monkeys on one side stop mixing with monkeys on the other. Give it enough time, and you get a whole new kind of howler.
Scientists say the Amazon, the Rio Branco and the Xingu did exactly that. Remember this. It matters on Day 100.

scenes.label: 150 m swim
scenes.say: This one's just a creek, though. And howlers can swim. One was once seen paddling across a river 150 meters wide.
So I jump. Dog paddle. Head up. Halfway across, two eyes pop up from the brown water. A caiman.
I have never swum so fast in my life. I grab a root, haul myself up, and climb till my arms shake.
Day 38. I'm starving, and I find something weird to eat. A termite nest, stuck to a tree trunk.
Red howlers really do this. We tear open termite nests and eat them, soil and all. Groups even come back to the same nest until nothing's left.
Then a gang of tufted capuchins swings in. Loud, fast, nosy. They steal everything. They also tell me where the fruit is.
I follow them to a fruiting tree. First real meal in days. But here's the thing. The trees are starting to thin out.
Day 45. The forest just stops. Like someone cut it with scissors. On the other side, flat fields, all the way to the sky.
This is the Arc of Deforestation, the southern edge of the Amazon, where forest gets cleared for farms, pasture and roads.
Cows where trees used to be. The forest is broken into islands now, and the islands don't touch.
For an animal that never wants to touch the ground, that's a nightmare. Every gap is a trap.
And I can hear them. Faint howls, from the next island of trees. Another group. Maybe my new family.
Day 52. Between me and those howls, there's a road. No branches over it. Nothing. Just open sky.
Howlers are safest high in the trees. Our worst moments happen when we cross open ground. And I have to go down.
So here we are. Back where this story began. My hands on red dirt. And that roar? It's a truck.
I panic and run the wrong way, straight back into my own trees. The truck thunders past, so close the dust buries me.
Then a dog barks from a farmhouse. I don't wait to see it. I'm twenty meters up before it reaches the trees.

scenes.label: 34% dog attacks
scenes.say: In one 20-year study of brown howlers in southern Brazil, dog attacks were 34 percent of all the injuries and deaths recorded.
Day 58. Okay, new idea. Above the road there are long black vines, stretched from tree to tree. Perfect. Right?
Wrong. Those aren't vines. They're power lines. And they're the deadliest shortcut a monkey can take.

scenes.label: 37% electrocution
scenes.say: In that same southern Brazil study, electrocution was number one. 37 percent of all the incidents, bigger than cars or dogs.
Touch two wires at once, and you close the circuit. Monkeys get badly hurt or killed. Sometimes it even knocks out the power for the whole area.
I stare at those wires for an hour. Then I turn around. Some days, surviving means not taking the shortcut.
Day 64. I wake up coughing. The air tastes like ash. Somewhere upwind, the forest is burning.

scenes.label: Lightning: under 1%
scenes.say: Here's what most people don't know. Rainforests barely burn on their own. Lightning starts less than 1 percent of Amazon fires.
Almost all of them are started by people. And in a drought year, one small fire can run wild.

scenes.label: 45.1 million hectares
scenes.say: And Mato Grosso, my state, has burned more than any other state in Brazil since 1985. 45.1 million hectares.
I climb toward the wind, away from the smoke, branch after branch, for hours. The fire doesn't reach my island. This time.
Day 71. The rains finally start. Everything turns green. And then come the mosquitoes. Clouds of them.
Howlers have a dark job in Brazil. We catch yellow fever from forest mosquitoes, and it hits us very hard.

scenes.label: 2,000+ howlers
scenes.say: In a 2008 to 2009 outbreak, over 2,000 howler monkeys died. Now health workers treat dead howlers as an early warning for people.
We don't spread it to people. We're the alarm bell. Kind of a sad superpower, but it saves human lives.
Day 77. At dawn, the new group roars again. Closer this time. So I do something brave. I roar back.
For the first time in weeks, someone answers me. They know I'm here. But the road is still between us.
I can't swim across a road. I can't climb the wires. I can't risk the ground again. So, what's left?
Day 83. That's when I see it. Ropes. Thick ropes and netting, strung high over the road, from forest to forest.

scenes.label: Canopy bridge
scenes.say: It's a canopy bridge. Real ones exist right here, near the town of Alta Floresta, built by a project called Reconecta.

scenes.label: 15,000 crossings
scenes.say: In 2024 they put up eight rope bridges. In 15 months, cameras counted 15,000 animal crossings, and not a single roadkill.
But I don't trust it. Ropes that don't move like branches? So I watch. The capuchins go first, of course.
In fact, near Alta Floresta, a capuchin crossed a brand-new bridge just two days after it went up. Show-offs.
Then tiny marmosets scurry across. Then a sloth, so slow it takes forever. Nothing falls. Nothing gets hit.
Day 90. My turn. I wrap my tail around the rope. Its tip is bare underneath, for grip, like a fifth hand.
Hand, hand, tail. Hand, hand, tail. Below me, a truck roars past. It can't touch me up here.
Halfway across, I hear a tiny click. A box on a pole is taking my picture. I have no idea what that photo will mean.
And then, leaves. Real branches. I'm across. I sit down and shake for a full minute. Then I roar.
Day 94. The group finds me. A big old male, three females, a little one riding on a back. They stare.
Nobody attacks. One female sits next to me. Then another. That night, I sleep in a cluster again. Warm.
Next morning, I'm part of the dawn roar. My voice, their voice, rolling out for kilometers. I'm home.
A few weeks later, I'll spot a female with a baby riding on her back. Maybe someday that'll be me. Maybe on that same bridge.
Day 100. Remember my question from the start? What did scientists say about me? Okay, here it is. This part is real.

scenes.label: New species!
scenes.say: On 30 October 2026, scientists announced two howler monkey species nobody had ever named. One lives exactly here.
Its name is Alouatta matogrossensis, the Mato Grosso red howler. It looked like other red howlers, but its DNA told a different story.

scenes.label: First in 84 years
scenes.say: The team compared the genomes of 11 howler species. It's the first new howler named in 84 years. Now there are 16.
And one real photo in the study shows a female of this species, with a baby on her back, crossing a canopy bridge in Brazil.
The bad news? Scientists say it may already be on the brink. Its home is one of the fastest-deforesting regions on Earth.

scenes.label: Lowest since 1988
scenes.say: The good news? Amazon forest loss just hit its lowest since records began in 1988. In Mato Grosso, it fell 46.7 percent in a year.
So here's my lesson. Sometimes survival isn't being the strongest. It's a few ropes, in the right place, at the right time.
Now your turn. Would you have tried the power lines, the ground, or waited for the bridge? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: Nobody Had Named This Monkey. Now It's Stuck on a Road
short.description: The Mato Grosso red howler was only named in October 2026. Full Day 1 to Day 100 story on the channel.

scenes.say: Nobody had even named this monkey until weeks ago. Now it's stuck on a road.
It's a Mato Grosso red howler. In October 2026, DNA proved it's a brand-new species, the first new howler in 84 years.
Its forest is being cut into islands. To find a new family, a young howler has to cross gaps like this one.
The wires look like vines. They're the deadliest shortcut. In one Brazilian study, electrocution caused 37 percent of howler incidents.
So people built rope bridges over the roads. Eight bridges near Alta Floresta logged 15,000 crossings in 15 months, with zero roadkill.
Does she make it across? Full 100-day story on my channel. Because nobody had even named this monkey until weeks ago. Now it's stuck on a road.
